questions.title: Who opens the stomata?
questions.text: Identify the part that controls the closing and opening of the stomatal pore in leaves of plants.
steps: ① The stoma is just the pore (the hole) ✗
② Two kidney-shaped guard cells surround it
③ Water enters guard cells ⟹ they swell ⟹ pore opens
④ Water leaves ⟹ they shrink ⟹ pore closes
∴ Guard cells → (c)
questions.remember: Stomata open when guard cells swell with water and close when they lose water. Stomata allow gas exchange and transpiration.
questions.trap: Picking 'stomata': the stoma is the pore itself; the guard cells around it do the controlling.
questions.ncert: NCERT Ch 5 · Section 5.2.1 (Fig. 5.3 open and closed stomatal pore)
questions.tryit: Why do stomata close on a very hot, dry afternoon?
questions.tryans: To reduce water loss by transpiration

questions.title: Which chamber pumps oxygen-rich blood?
questions.text: In human beings, the oxygen-rich blood is pumped out to the body by:
steps: ① Oxygen-rich blood returns from the lungs to the LEFT side
② Left atrium → left ventricle
③ Pumping out = CONTRACTION (relaxing only fills)
④ The thick-walled left ventricle contracts ⟹ blood goes to the body
∴ Contraction of left ventricle → (d)
questions.remember: Right side: deoxygenated blood (body → right atrium → right ventricle → lungs). Left side: oxygenated (lungs → left atrium → left ventricle → body).
questions.trap: Picking 'relaxation': a chamber FILLS when it relaxes and PUMPS when it contracts.
questions.ncert: NCERT Ch 5 · Section 5.4.1 (Fig. 5.10 the human heart)
questions.tryit: Why does the left ventricle have the thickest wall?
questions.tryans: It pumps blood to the whole body, so it needs the most force

questions.title: The events of photosynthesis
questions.text:
The following events occur during the process of photosynthesis. Choose the option that indicates the correct events.
(i) Oxidation of carbon dioxide to carbohydrates
(ii) Conversion of light energy into chemical energy
(iii) Absorption of light energy by chlorophyll
(iv) Conversion of hydrogen and oxygen into water
steps: ① Event 1: chlorophyll absorbs light ⟹ (iii) ✓
② Event 2: light energy → chemical energy; water is split ⟹ (ii) ✓
③ Event 3: CO₂ is REDUCED to carbohydrate ⟹ (i) 'oxidation' ✗
④ Water is split, not made from H and O ⟹ (iv) ✗
∴ (ii) and (iii) → (b)
questions.remember: Three events: (1) chlorophyll absorbs light; (2) light → chemical energy and water splits into H and O; (3) CO₂ is reduced to carbohydrates.
questions.trap: Picking (i): carbon dioxide is REDUCED (gains hydrogen) to make carbohydrate, not oxidised.
questions.tryit: Which gas is released in photosynthesis, and where does it come from?
questions.tryans: Oxygen, from the splitting of water

questions.title: Assertion–Reason: do arteries have valves?
questions.text:
Assertion (A): Arteries have valves as they have to withstand high pressure.
Reason (R): Arteries are vessels which carry blood away from the heart to various organs.
opts: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
steps: ① Arteries carry blood AWAY from the heart ✓ R true
② Blood leaves the heart under high pressure
③ So arteries have THICK, ELASTIC walls, not valves
④ Valves are in VEINS (low pressure, stop backflow) ⟹ A false
∴ A false, R true → (d)
questions.ans: Option (d) A is false, but R is true
questions.remember: Arteries: away from the heart, high pressure, thick elastic walls, no valves. Veins: towards the heart, low pressure, thin walls, valves stop backflow.
questions.trap: Accepting A because 'high pressure' sounds right. The fix for high pressure is thick walls; valves are a vein feature.
questions.tryans: Blood in veins is at low pressure; valves stop it flowing backwards

questions.title: Double circulation, step by step
questions.text: Briefly mention the steps in double circulation through the human heart.
steps: ① Body → vena cava → right atrium (deoxygenated)
② Right atrium → right ventricle → lungs (O₂ taken in)
③ Lungs → left atrium (oxygenated)
④ Left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → body
⑤ Blood passes through the heart TWICE per cycle
∴ Pulmonary + systemic = double circulation
questions.ans: Body → right atrium → right ventricle → lungs → left atrium → left ventricle → body: blood passes through the heart twice in one cycle
questions.remember: Double circulation keeps oxygenated and deoxygenated blood separate, giving a highly efficient O₂ supply: needed by warm-blooded mammals and birds.
questions.trap: Writing only the chambers. Name the two routes: heart → lungs → heart (pulmonary) and heart → body → heart (systemic).
questions.tryit: Why do mammals and birds need double circulation?
questions.tryans: They are warm-blooded and need a lot of energy, so O₂-rich and O₂-poor blood must not mix

questions.title: Which respiration gives more energy?
questions.text: What kind of respiration provides more energy and why?
steps: ① Aerobic respiration (with oxygen) gives more energy
② In mitochondria, glucose breaks down COMPLETELY
③ Glucose → pyruvate → CO₂ + H₂O + a lot of ATP
④ Anaerobic: incomplete breakdown (lactic acid or ethanol)
∴ Aerobic: complete breakdown releases more energy
questions.ans: Aerobic respiration: glucose is broken down completely to CO₂ and water in the mitochondria, releasing much more energy
questions.remember: Aerobic: cytoplasm + mitochondria, CO₂ + H₂O, much energy. Anaerobic: cytoplasm only, ethanol + CO₂ (yeast) or lactic acid (muscles), little energy.
questions.trap: Writing only 'aerobic' without the WHY: the second mark is for 'complete breakdown of glucose'.
questions.tryit: What causes muscle cramps after hard exercise?
questions.tryans: Lactic acid builds up from anaerobic respiration in muscles

questions.title: How water climbs a plant
questions.text: In xylem tissue, vessels and tracheids of the roots, stems and leaves are interconnected to form a continuous system of water-conducting channels reaching all parts of the plant. Explain how this is achieved.
steps: ① Root cells take in ions from the soil actively
② This creates a concentration difference: water enters the root
③ Water is pushed up the xylem: root pressure (mainly at night)
④ Leaves lose water through stomata: transpiration
⑤ This creates a suction: transpiration pull draws water up
∴ Root pressure + transpiration pull move water up the xylem
questions.ans: Root cells take up ions, so water enters the root and is pushed up (root pressure); water lost by transpiration from leaves creates a suction (transpiration pull) that draws water up the continuous xylem
questions.remember: Root pressure matters most at night; in the day, transpiration pull is the main force. Transpiration also helps absorb minerals and cools the leaf.
questions.trap: Mentioning only transpiration. Explain BOTH: root pressure from ion uptake, and the transpiration pull.
questions.ncert: NCERT Ch 5 · Section 5.4.2 Transportation in plants
questions.tryit: Why is transpiration called a 'necessary evil'?
questions.tryans: It wastes water, but it pulls water and minerals up and cools the plant
